newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Peace crisis, scandal hit Netanyahu economy plans. [CORRECTED 13:01 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Peace crisis, scandal hit Netanyahu economy plans. [CORRECTED 13:01 GMT]

text.p: It's the peace process, stupid.

That's the bottom line for analysts asked to explain why Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, hit by peace crises and political scandal, has been slow to deliver on many of his sweeping economic promises after a year in office.
"In Israel, there is always something more burning than the economy," Doron Tsur, head of research at Sahar Securities, said on Wednesday. "He has gotten entangled in a lot of trouble."

The U.S.-educated Netanyahu needed no writing on the wall before last May's election to teach him that even in embattled Israel it's the economy that is a key issue in a country with a workforce swollen by immigration and increasingly accustomed to ever-rising standards of living.

He pledged to fire up the engine of economic revolution in his first year in office by reforming capital markets, speeding up privatisation and deregulating public transport, telecommunications, television and land ownership.
One year later, analysts give Netanyahu passing marks on state sell-offs but say he has fallen short on other reforms.
"At the end of the day, politics always gets in the way and that's probably precluded him from doing what he wanted to do," said Stephen Levey of Carnegie Emerging Markets in London.
A member of his own government, Immigration Minister Yuli Edelstein was scathing in criticism published on Wednesday.

"The prime minister promised again and again when he took office that he would turn the Israeli economy from a corner grocery into a supermarket," he told the Haaretz newspaper. "But nothing has really happened.

"For months, everything has been delayed. When things are frozen on the political side, they explode right away. It could take six months before economic matters blow up and then everyone will recall that a year ago no one took any decisions -- not about (high) interest rates or capital markets."
Netanyahu's list of priorities has tilted heavily towards putting out political fires rather than reforming a slowing economy.

In September, Netanyahu touched off clashes with the Palestinians by opening a new entrance to an archaelogical tunnel near Moslem holy sites in East Jerusalem. Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
(Corrects death toll from sixty-one Israelis and 15 Palestinians).
Relations with the Palestinians and Arab world plunged into deep crisis in March when work began on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem.

Netanyahu is still recovering from a political scandal over his short-lived appointment of an attorney-general who prosecutors charged was backed by a coalition ally hoping to cut a deal in an on-going corruption trial.

"Much about the economy is connected to the peace process: the psychology, the mood. When there is a feeling that things are stuck, it affects everything," Tsur said. "I don't think that during the three months of the (scandal), he focused on how to take care of exporters, for example."

The government failed to implement controversial proposals to reform Israel's volatile capital markets by encouraging more long-term savings. Plans to undertake structural reforms to enhance competition in transport and the media have been approved in principle but nothing concrete has been done.
However in telecommunications, the government has awarded two licences to operate international phone service in competition with state-controlled monopoly Bezeq.
"Privatisations are going okay -- Bank Leumi and Bank Discount. But the truth is that they were in the pipeline for five years," Tsur said.

"He's done well so far...but I think El Al will prove more difficult," Levey said, referring to Israel's national airline that could be a hard sell because it does not fly on the Jewish Sabbath and is saddled with high security costs.

A secondary offering in Israel Discount Bank was made in April and 17 percent of Israel Chemicals Ltd was sold to Israel Corp in March for $200 million. A $150 million secondary offering in Bank Leumi is due to take place next week.
The government expects to raise four billion shekels from privatisations this year.

"We are in an accelerated process of privatisation. We have privatised close to 1.5 billion shekels in the last two months," Netanyahu told members of his Likud party earlier this month. "We are on the verge of privatising Bank Hapoalim."
Last month, Israel approved a plan to sell 25 percent of Bezeq that would reduce the government's holding to 51 percent.
But analysts pointed to a general malaise in Israel and confusion abroad over just where Netanyahu is headed in a peace process that colours the economic mood in the Jewish state.
"After a year, I think it's time the world knew exactly where he stands on the peace process," Levey said. "Enough dithering already."
($1 = 3.39 shekels)
